Widespread wrongdoing and the coming Chaldeans (verses 1–11)

The Lord's servants are deeply distressed when they see irreverence and violence prevail, especially among people who profess to know the truth.

People had become willing to injure their neighbors without hesitation.

We should long for the world in which holiness and love reign forever and violence will never again be seen.

God has wise reasons both for showing patience toward wicked people and for allowing his faithful servants to express their concern.

The day will come when the cry raised by wrongdoing will testify against those who committed it, while the prayers of people who suffered wrong will be heard on their behalf.

God's people were to watch what was happening among the surrounding nations, especially the rise of the Chaldeans.

They were to understand that their own land would be punished through that nation.

Yet many people assume their prosperity must continue indefinitely.

Others expect disaster to happen only after their own lifetime.

The Chaldeans were a bitter, swift, violent and merciless people.

Their forces would overwhelm those who opposed them.

But they would also commit a serious sin common among the proud: claiming all the glory of success for themselves.

The conclusion of the prophecy nevertheless contained a glimpse of comfort for God's people.

God's holiness even when a worse nation prospers (verses 12–17)

Whatever happens around us, the Lord remains our God and our Holy One.

We have offended him, but we must not therefore entertain unjust or harsh thoughts about him or his service.

It is deeply comforting that human beings may intend evil while the Lord intends good.

His counsel will stand.

Even if wicked people prosper for a time, God remains perfectly holy and does not approve of their evil.

He cannot commit injustice, nor can he look on wickedness with approval.

We must hold to this principle even when temporary events seem difficult to reconcile with it.

Habakkuk complained that people were abusing God's patience.

Because punishment did not follow their crimes immediately, their hearts grew bolder in doing wrong.

The conquerors caught some victims one by one, like fish taken on a hook; they gathered others in nets and drag-nets, capturing whole groups together.

They admired their skill and strategy.

We are all inclined to take credit for our success and good fortune.

When people worship the clever methods that made them successful, they are sacrificing to their own nets—making idols of themselves.

God will bring their impressive robberies to an end.

Death and judgment will stop those who prey upon others; in turn, they themselves will face judgment.

Whatever advantages we possess, let us give all glory to God.
classic_reading:
[Hab.1.1-Hab.1.11]
Habakkuk
The subject of this prophecy is the destruction of Judea and Jerusalem for the sins of the people, and the consolation of the faithful under national calamities.
Chapter 1
Chapter Outline
The wickedness of the land. The fearful vengeance to be executed. | (1-11) |
These judgments to be inflicted by a nation more wicked than themselves. | (12-17) |
Verses 1-11
The servants of the Lord are deeply afflicted by seeing ungodliness and violence prevail; especially among those who profess the truth. No man scrupled doing wrong to his neighbour. We should long to remove to the world where holiness and love reign for ever, and no violence shall be before us. God has good reasons for his long-suffering towards bad men, and the rebukes of good men. The day will come when the cry of sin will be heard against those that do wrong, and the cry of prayer for those that suffer wrong. They were to notice what was going forward among the heathen by the Chaldeans, and to consider themselves a nation to be scourged by them. But most men presume on continued prosperity, or that calamities will not come in their days. They are a bitter and hasty nation, fierce, cruel, and bearing down all before them. They shall overcome all that oppose them. But it is a great offence, and the common offence of proud people, to take glory to themselves. The closing words give a glimpse of comfort.
[Hab.1.12-Hab.1.17]
Verses 12-17
However matters may be, yet God is the Lord our God, our Holy One. We are an offending people, he is an offended God, yet we will not entertain hard thoughts of him, or of his service. It is great comfort that, whatever mischief men design, the Lord designs good, and we are sure that his counsel shall stand. Though wickedness may prosper a while, yet God is holy, and does not approve the wickedness. As he cannot do iniquity himself, so he is of purer eyes than to behold it with any approval. By this principle we must abide, though the dispensations of his providence may for a time, in some cases, seem to us not to agree with it. The prophet complains that God's patience was abused; and because sentence against these evil works and workers was not executed speedily, their hearts were the more fully set in them to do evil. Some they take up as with the angle, one by one; others they catch in shoals, as in their net, and gather them in their drag, their enclosing net. They admire their own cleverness and contrivance: there is great proneness in us to take the glory of outward prosperity to ourselves. This is idolizing ourselves, sacrificing to the drag-net because it is our own. God will soon end successful and splendid robberies. Death and judgment shall make men cease to prey on others, and they shall be preyed on themselves. Let us remember, whatever advantages we possess, we must give all the glory to God.

Waiting for the Lord in faith (verses 1–4)

When we are troubled and uncertain about the ways of God's Providence, we must guard against the temptation to become impatient.

After presenting our complaints and requests to him, we should watch for the answer he gives through his word, Spirit and providential dealings.

What is the Lord saying to our situation?

God will not disappoint the faith of those who wait to hear his reply.

Every person is concerned with the truths contained in God's word.

The promised blessing may seem delayed for a long time, but it will come at last.

The result will more than repay the patient waiting of his people.

A humble and repentant sinner seeks an interest in this salvation.

Such a person rests upon God's promise and upon Christ, through whom that promise is fulfilled.

They not only live by faith, but also walk and work by faith, persevering until the end and receiving glory.

Those who distrust or despise God's complete sufficiency do not live uprightly before him.

The righteous shall live by faith in these precious promises even while they await their fulfillment.

Those who are justified by faith will truly live and enjoy God's blessing now and forever.

Warnings against the greed and oppression of Chaldea (verses 5–14)

The prophet announced judgment against proud, violent powers that oppress God's people.

Human beings become ensnared through the desires of the flesh, the desires of the eyes and the pride of life.

The power that had carried Israel into captivity was itself captive to these sinful desires.

We should regard only what was honestly acquired as properly ours.

Riches are like thick clay.

Gold and silver are no more than differently colored earth.

Traveling through deep mud slows a person down and makes the journey dirty.

So people who surround themselves with riches may find their progress burdened and polluted.

How foolish it is to carry such a heavy load of anxiety, guilt from acquiring and spending it, and accountability before God!

People can become so weighed down by wealth that it drags them toward destruction.

What was taken violently from others may be taken violently from the thief in turn.

Greed brings disturbance to a household.

A person greedy for gain brings trouble upon the family.

Worse, fraud and injustice call down divine judgment upon the household's affairs.

Honest gain may support a family with God's blessing.

Dishonest gain instead tends toward poverty, ruin and spiritual danger.

Those who injure their neighbors do still greater injury to their own souls.

The possessions they have accumulated will testify against them, however carefully their frauds were planned.

Few people endure a worse slavery than those devoted entirely to worldly pursuits.

They are disappointed when they fail to obtain wealth and disappointed again when they possess it.

They finally discover that the result was not merely emptiness but distress of spirit.

By humiliating the world's pretended glory, God displays his own true glory.

The whole earth will be filled with its knowledge as the waters cover the sea.

Drunkenness, exploitation and idolatry judged (verses 15–20)

The Lord pronounced severe judgment against drunkenness everywhere, from a royal palace to the smallest tavern.

Giving a thirsty or exhausted person a drink can be a work of mercy.

But deliberately making another person drunk in order to expose them, discover private matters, trap them into a bad bargain or use them for some other evil purpose is serious wickedness.

To enjoy this sin is to contribute to the destruction of both body and soul.

Punishment will correspond to the offense.

The prophet also showed the foolishness of worshiping idols.

The Lord dwells in his holy heavenly temple.

He allows us to approach him in the way he has appointed.

May we welcome his salvation and worship him through Jesus Christ and the work of the Holy Spirit.
classic_reading:
[Hab.2.1-Hab.2.4]
Chapter 2
Chapter Outline
Habakkuk must wait in faith. | (1-4) |
Judgments upon the Chaldeans. | (5-14) |
Also upon drunkenness and idolatry. | (15-20) |
Verses 1-4
When tossed and perplexed with doubts about the methods of Providence, we must watch against temptations to be impatient. When we have poured out complaints and requests before God, we must observe the answers God gives by his word, his Spirit, and providences; what the Lord will say to our case. God will not disappoint the believing expectations of those who wait to hear what he will say unto them. All are concerned in the truths of God's word. Though the promised favour be deferred long, it will come at last, and abundantly recompense us for waiting. The humble, broken-hearted, repenting sinner, alone seeks to obtain an interest in this salvation. He will rest his soul on the promise, and on Christ, in and through whom it is given. Thus he walks and works, as well as lives by faith, perseveres to the end, and is exalted to glory; while those who distrust or despise God's all-sufficiency will not walk uprightly with him. The just shall live by faith in these precious promises, while the performance of them is deferred. Only those made just by faith, shall live, shall be happy here and for ever.
[Hab.2.5-Hab.2.14]
Verses 5-14
The prophet reads the doom of all proud and oppressive powers that bear hard upon God's people. The lusts of the flesh, the lust of the eye, and the pride of life, are the entangling snares of men; and we find him that led Israel captive, himself led captive by each of these. No more of what we have is to be reckoned ours, than what we come honestly by. Riches are but clay, thick clay; what are gold and silver but white and yellow earth? Those who travel through thick clay, are hindered and dirtied in their journey; so are those who go through the world in the midst of abundance of wealth. And what fools are those that burden themselves with continual care about it; with a great deal of guilt in getting, saving, and spending it, and with a heavy account which they must give another day! They overload themselves with this thick clay, and so sink themselves down into destruction and perdition. See what will be the end hereof; what is gotten by violence from others, others shall take away by violence. Covetousness brings disquiet and uneasiness into a family; he that is greedy of gain troubles his own house; what is worse, it brings the curse of God upon all the affairs of it. There is a lawful gain, which, by the blessing of God, may be a comfort to a house; but what is got by fraud and injustice, will bring poverty and ruin upon a family. Yet that is not the worst; Thou hast sinned against thine own soul, hast endangered it. Those who wrong their neighbours, do much greater wrong to their own souls. If the sinner thinks he has managed his frauds and violence with art and contrivance, the riches and possessions he heaped together will witness against him. There are not greater drudges in the world than those who are slaves to mere wordly pursuits. And what comes of it? They find themselves disappointed of it, and disappointed in it; they will own it is worse than vanity, it is vexation of spirit. By staining and sinking earthly glory, God manifests and magnifies his own glory, and fills the earth with the knowledge of it, as plentifully as waters cover the sea, which are deep, and spread far and wide.
[Hab.2.15-Hab.2.20]
Verses 15-20
A severe woe is pronounced against drunkenness; it is very fearful against all who are guilty of drunkenness at any time, and in any place, from the stately palace to the paltry ale-house. To give one drink who is in want, who is thirsty and poor, or a weary traveller, or ready to perish, is charity; but to give a neighbour drink, that he may expose himself, may disclose secret concerns, or be drawn into a bad bargain, or for any such purpose, this is wickedness. To be guilty of this sin, to take pleasure in it, is to do what we can towards the murder both of soul and body. There is woe to him, and punishment answering to the sin. The folly of worshipping idols is exposed. The Lord is in his holy temple in heaven, where we have access to him in the way he has appointed. May we welcome his salvation, and worship him in his earthly temples, through Christ Jesus, and by the influence of the Holy Spirit.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe prophet beseeches God for his people.1, 2He calls to mind former deliverances.3–15His firm trust in the Divine mercy.16–19
Habakkuk prays for God's mercy (verses 1 and 2)

Here the word prayer appears to describe an act of devoted worship.

The prophet asks the Lord to renew his work among the people in the midst of years of trouble.

This prayer can be applied whenever the church, or individual believers, suffer afflictions and trials.

We must flee to God's mercy as our refuge.

It is the only ground on which we may plead for his help.

We must not say, “Remember what we deserve.”

We should say, “Lord, remember your own mercy.”

Remembering God's earlier deliverances (verses 3–15)

When God's people experience trouble and feel near despair, they should recall what he did in earlier generations.

They can bring those acts before him in prayer.

The resemblance between the captivity in Babylon and the earlier slavery in Egypt encourages hope that the Lord can deliver again.

God revealed himself in glory.

The powers of nature trembled and their usual course was altered.

All this served the salvation of his people.

Even events that appear least likely to help will be made to serve their deliverance.

These past victories were also pictures of the world's redemption through Jesus Christ.

The prophet spoke of salvation with God's anointed.

Joshua, who led Israel in battle, was a figure of the Savior who bears the corresponding name—Jesus, our true Joshua.

Henry understands the ancient acts of salvation as accomplished by God with reference to Christ, the Anointed One.

All the earlier wonders performed for Israel were surpassed by what happened when the Son of God suffered on the cross for his people's sins.

How glorious his resurrection and ascension were!

How much more glorious his return will be, when he puts an end to everything that opposes him and brings suffering to his people!

Joy in the Lord despite every outward loss (verses 16–19)

When trouble approaches, we need to prepare.

A sound hope through grace is accompanied by a holy fear.

Habakkuk recalled what God had done in former times.

As he considered those deliverances, his confidence returned and his heart filled with holy joy.

He decided to delight and triumph in the Lord.

Even if he lost everything else, he would not lose his God.

If the vines and fig trees fail, all the pleasures of a merely worldly heart disappear.

But people who enjoyed God when everything was plentiful can continue to find everything they need in him after possessions vanish.

They can sit among the ruins of their earthly comforts and still praise the Lord as the God of their salvation.

They rejoice in the salvation of their souls, even through the deepest distress.

Joy in the Lord is especially appropriate when losses and troubles surround us.

Even when food is lacking, showing that human beings do not live by bread alone, the Spirit can supply grace and consolation.

God's gifts make us strong for spiritual work and warfare.

With hearts enlarged by grace, we can run in the way of his commandments and rise above our troubles.

The prophet began his prayer in fear and trembling and ended in joy and triumph.

Faith in Christ prepares believers for every circumstance.

When we can speak of Jesus as our Savior, his name becomes medicine for every wound and refreshment in every care.

It is like fragrant perfume filling the soul.

Hoping for the crown of heaven, let us hold earthly possessions lightly and bear suffering with cheerful patience.

In a little while, the One who is coming will come, and we will be where he is.
classic_reading:
[Hab.3.1-Hab.3.2]
Chapter 3
Chapter Outline
The prophet beseeches God for his people. | (1-2) |
He calls to mind former deliverances. | (3-15) |
His firm trust in the Divine mercy. | (16-19) |
Verses 1-2
The word prayer seems used here for an act of devotion. The Lord would revive his work among the people in the midst of the years of adversity. This may be applied to every season when the church, or believers, suffer under afflictions and trials. Mercy is what we must flee to for refuge, and rely upon as our only plea. We must not say, Remember our merit, but, Lord, remember thy own mercy.
[Hab.3.3-Hab.3.15]
Verses 3-15
God's people, when in distress, and ready to despair, seek help by considering the days of old, and the years of ancient times, and by pleading them with God in prayer. The resemblance between the Babylonish and Egyptian captivities, naturally presents itself to the mind, as well as the possibility of a like deliverance through the power of Jehovah. God appeared in his glory. All the powers of nature are shaken, and the course of nature changed, but all is for the salvation of God's own people. Even what seems least likely, shall be made to work for their salvation. Hereby is given a type and figure of the redemption of the world by Jesus Christ. It is for salvation with thine anointed. Joshua who led the armies of Israel, was a figure of Him whose name he bare, even Jesus, our Joshua. In all the salvations wrought for them, God looked upon Christ the Anointed, and brought deliverances to pass by him. All the wonders done for Israel of old, were nothing to that which was done when the Son of God suffered on the cross for the sins of his people. How glorious his resurrection and ascension! And how much more glorious will be his second coming, to put an end to all that opposes him, and all that causes suffering to his people!
[Hab.3.16-Hab.3.19]
Verses 16-19
When we see a day of trouble approach, it concerns us to prepare. A good hope through grace is founded in holy fear. The prophet looked back upon the experiences of the church in former ages, and observed what great things God had done for them, and so was not only recovered, but filled with holy joy. He resolved to delight and triumph in the Lord; for when all is gone, his God is not gone. Destroy the vines and the fig-trees, and you make all the mirth of a carnal heart to cease. But those who, when full, enjoyed God in all, when emptied and poor, can enjoy all in God. They can sit down upon the heap of the ruins of their creature-comforts, and even then praise the Lord, as the God of their salvation, the salvation of the soul, and rejoice in him as such, in their greatest distresses. Joy in the Lord is especially seasonable when we meet with losses and crosses in the world. Even when provisions are cut off, to make it appear that man lives not by bread alone, we may be supplied by the graces and comforts of God's Spirit. Then we shall be strong for spiritual warfare and work, and with enlargement of heart may run the way of his commandments, and outrun our troubles. And we shall be successful in spiritual undertakings. Thus the prophet, who began his prayer with fear and trembling, ends it with joy and triumph. And thus faith in Christ prepares for every event. The name of Jesus, when we can speak of Him as ours, is balm for every wound, a cordial for every care. It is as ointment poured forth, shedding fragrance through the whole soul. In the hope of a heavenly crown, let us sit loose to earthly possessions and comforts, and cheerfully bear up under crosses. Yet a little while, and He that shall come will come, and will not tarry; and where he is, we shall be also.
